issues.subcategory: retrospective design mislabeled as prospective
issues.description: The authors repeatedly claim a 'prospective research design' overcoming power issues of a 'true prospective study,' but the design is fundamentally retrospective: participants reconstruct past episodes from memory and data is analyzed retrospectively. The communication data may be archival, but episode dating and classification are retrospective, which undermines temporal/causal inference about escalation toward attempts.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a ‘true’ prospective study design.

issues.subcategory: contradictory results reporting between sections
issues.description: The discussion claims the high-risk period was associated with greater anxiety and sadness, but the Results (Primary Analysis 1) explicitly state no significant effect emerged for anxiety, and sadness was significant only versus ideation. This is a direct contradiction between results and discussion, and the abstract only mentions anger/positive emotion. The repeated mention of 'anxiety' as elevated is unsupported by the reported tests.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.subcategory: inconsistent test statistic values across sections
issues.description: The anger interaction chi-square reported in the text differs from Table 3. The Results text reports a significant interaction for anger but provides no chi-square value in one place, while Table 3 lists 2=7.83, p=.049. Additionally the text reports anger pairwise p-values (e.g., p=.0111) inconsistently formatted, and the death effect text says no significant differences with 'zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739' while Table 3 shows a pairwise z up to 1.83 with p=.067, and Positive vs. Attempt z=-0.82 p=.412 — the stated range '.067-.739' omits the .412 value, indicating inconsistency.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for anger words, such that anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types, including ideation (z=2.00, p=.046), depressed (z=2.49, p=.013), and positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes

issues.subcategory: directional inconsistency between coefficients and narrative
issues.description: For positive emotion, the narrative says positive emotion 'decreased more steeply during attempt episodes,' yet the Table 3 coefficients for Attempt vs. other episodes are positive (e.g., 0.027, 0.016, 0.010). For anger, the narrative says anger 'increased more steeply during attempt' but the coefficients are negative (-0.023, -0.026, -0.027). The sign of the coefficients relative to the stated direction is not explained, making it impossible to verify the claimed directions without clarification of the coding/reference scheme.
issues.quote: There was a significant interaction for positive emotion, 2(3)=41.67, p<.001, such that positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes compared to all other episode types

issues.subcategory: operationalization mismatch for suicide attempt
issues.description: The central outcome 'suicide attempt' is operationalized to include episodes in which no physical attempt occurred and even cases relying solely on subjective self-endorsement on a screener. 71% of 'attempts' involved no physical harm. This substantially weakens the construct validity of the 'high risk/suicide attempt' category that anchors the entire design and undermines the claim of studying behaviors 'most strongly associated with suicide completion.'
issues.quote: Note that reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.

issues.subcategory: construct not measured matching its definition
issues.description: The social engagement construct is theoretically tied to perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness (interpersonal theory), but is operationalized only as counts/ratios of sent vs. received messages. This crude proxy does not capture burdensomeness or belongingness, so a null result cannot test the theoretical hypothesis. The authors acknowledge this only partially in discussion but still framed it as a test of the interpersonal theory.
issues.quote: In the current study, we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

issues.subcategory: post hoc selection of time window presented as a priori
issues.description: The two-week episode window is justified both a priori (Millner et al.) and empirically via 'visual inspection of descriptive figures' to identify where rate of change appeared most pronounced. Using the same data to choose the analysis window introduces circularity/researcher degrees of freedom that can inflate the temporal interaction effects, which are the paper's headline findings.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.subcategory: no multiple comparisons correction with many tests
issues.description: The authors run a large number of tests (multiple LIWC variables × mean and slope models × pairwise comparisons) and deliberately apply no correction, while several 'significant' results have p-values just under .05 (e.g., .049, .046, .033, .035, .024). With borderline p-values and many tests, the risk of false positives is high; the justification (Rothman 1990) is debatable for confirmatory claims, and the borderline anger result (p=.049 omnibus) is particularly fragile.
issues.quote: we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats

issues.subcategory: power analysis assumptions and inconsistent sample numbers
issues.description: The power analysis assumes large between-subjects effects for a within-subjects design (acknowledged as unknown), and the sample size accounting is confusing/inconsistent: '30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected usable SMS data, divided by the design effect).' Elsewhere 15 participants had attempt data and 21 attempts had SMS data. The numbers (20 vs 21 attempts with SMS, 30 vs 33 vs 15) are not reconciled, and the 'divided by the design effect' calculation is not specified, making the power claim non-reproducible.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes

issues.subcategory: inconsistent participant/episode counts
issues.description: The numbers describing attempt data are internally inconsistent. The text states 15 participants had data from at least one reported suicide attempt, but then reports 13 with single attempt and 14 with multiple among attempters with SMS data (13+14=27, not 15), and '21 attempts with corresponding SMS data.' These counts cannot be reconciled and confuse how many participants/attempts actually contributed to the key attempt analyses.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt... Among attempters with SMS data, 13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple (M=1.74, SD=0.86). Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data

issues.subcategory: substantial unaddressed data loss and selection bias
issues.description: Only 134 of 293 episodes (46%) had SMS data, and only 15 of 33 participants contributed attempt data. The reasons for missing SMS (iPhone encryption, lost devices, forgotten passwords) are likely non-random (e.g., related to phone type, time since attempt). This systematic missingness could bias which episodes are represented, yet the analysis treats it as benign 'missing data' handled by mixed models, which assumes MAR/ignorability that is not justified.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.subcategory: iatrogenic effect interpretation / inconsistent table values
issues.description: The text reports desire to die means (pre 0.82, post 0.61) and a significant decrease t(32)=2.23, p=.033, but Table 1 reports the iatrogenic change in desire to die as +0.20 (an increase), contradicting the in-text decrease of -0.21. Mood change is reported as -0.20 in the table consistent with text, but the desire-to-die sign is inconsistent. This is a direct numeric contradiction.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=0.61, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033

issues.subcategory: narrow sample extrapolated to broad claims
issues.description: The sample is overwhelmingly young (M=20.4), female (84.8%), college students recruited from a psychology pool, with mostly non-injurious 'attempts.' Yet the paper makes broad claims about real-time suicide risk markers and clinical monitoring tools. The mismatch between this narrow sample and the sweeping clinical/public-health framing constitutes generalizability overreach, especially given males are far more likely to die by suicide.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: overstated predictive/biomarker language from exploratory correlational data
issues.description: The paper repeatedly frames correlational, retrospective, within-subject differences as 'real-time digital biomarkers,' 'novel predictors of suicidal behaviors,' and identification of risk 'in real time,' despite no prospective prediction being performed. The slopes are associations across reconstructed episodes, not validated predictors. Terms like 'biomarker' and 'predicted' overstate the causal/predictive warrant.
issues.quote: This laboratory investigation identified novel predictors of suicidal behaviors, which may be utilized in the future by machine learning models to predict acute suicide risk

issues.subcategory: misstated statistical claim about prior model
issues.description: The claim that a risk model 'accounted for 80.3% of the variance' for a rare binary outcome is almost certainly a misinterpretation (likely AUC, classification accuracy, or pseudo-R2/area under curve), not variance explained. Misreporting this inflates the apparent state of risk prediction and frames the study's rationale incorrectly.
issues.quote: a recent model, which included known risk factors for suicide attempt, accounted for 80.3% of the variance (Nock, Borges, & Ono, 2012)

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding and single-experimenter classification
issues.description: Episode dating and classification were obtained by interview, and recruitment/data collection were performed by a single individual (J.J.G.) who also performed analyses. There is no mention of blinding the episode classification to the language data or independent verification of episode coding, raising risk of expectancy/confirmation bias in the key predictor variable.
issues.quote: Recruitment and data collection were performed by J.J.G. ... and J.J.G. performed the data analysis under the supervision of B.A.T.

issues.subcategory: LIWC limitations undermining sentiment construct
issues.description: LIWC counts isolated words without handling negation or context (the authors note 'not happy' counts as positive emotion). Since sentiment is the central construct yielding the headline findings (positive emotion, anger), this measurement limitation directly threatens the validity of the key results, not just future directions.
issues.quote: examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., “not happy” would count as “positive emotion” because negation is not accounted for)

issues.subcategory: missing detail on number of messages/days per episode and convergence
issues.description: Key reporting gaps prevent replication: the models that did not converge led to dropping random slopes ('Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included'), but the final random-effects structure, message-level n per episode, and handling of episodes with sparse days are not fully specified. The day variable ranges -14 to 0 but episodes vary in message density; how empty days were treated is unstated.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: underpowered subgroup for key interaction analyses
issues.description: The headline temporal (slope) findings rest on only ~15 participants/21 attempts contributing attempt-episode data, with pairwise comparisons (e.g., attempt vs. positive for self-focus, z=0.89) likely severely underpowered. Conclusions about effects being 'unique to attempts' versus shared with ideation/positive rely on null pairwise comparisons that the study is not powered to interpret as evidence of absence.
issues.quote: self-focus appeared to change over time differently for attempts compared to ideation and depressed, but not positive, episodes, suggesting self-focus did not uniquely distinguish attempts from other episodes

issues.subcategory: contradictory framing of random effects and Type I/II error
issues.description: The methods state the maximal random effects model was used to 'protect against inflated Type I error,' while the discussion argues the near-maximal structure 'likely decreased the chances of Type I error' yet also that maximal structures 'can be overly conservative and lead to a significant loss of power.' These statements are in tension, and combined with the convergence-driven reduction of random slopes, the actual Type I/II error properties of the final models are unclear.
issues.quote: a maximal random effects model... was used to boost generalizability of the findings and protect against inflated Type I error rates.

issues.subcategory: overclaim of novelty
issues.description: The paper repeatedly asserts it is the first to analyze private text messaging for any clinical outcome, but the authors' own cited companion work (Nobles et al., 2018) used the same/related text-message data for suicide classification. The strong 'first to our knowledge' claims for both 'suicide or any other clinical outcome' are overstated given overlapping prior/concurrent work.
issues.quote: This was also the first study, to our knowledge, to collect and analyze private text messaging data for suicide (or any other clinical outcome).

issues.subcategory: implausible reference value
issues.description: Borges et al. (2010) citation lists pages '1,478-1628' which is internally implausible (start page greater range formatting) and the 0.3% figure is presented to justify '300 unselected individuals would be required to produce a single suicide attempt,' but 0.3% implies ~333 individuals per attempt; the rounding to 'at least 300' is loose but the derivation conflates 12-month prevalence with incidence in a way that is not carefully justified.
issues.quote: one recent study estimated 12-month presence of suicide attempt for adults at 0.3% (Borges et al., 2010), which would mean that at least 300 unselected individuals would be required to produce a single suicide attempt during a one-year follow-up period

issues.subcategory: unequal episode contribution and pseudoreplication risk
issues.description: Participants contributed widely varying numbers of episodes and messages (1,200-1,600 messages per episode, 3-12 episodes), and message-level modeling with ~189,478 messages risks treating non-independent messages as informative units, potentially inflating effective sample size and precision of fixed effects despite random intercepts. The degree to which a few prolific texters dominate estimates is not reported.
issues.quote: Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode.

issues.subcategory: no theoretical expectation of temporal change in comparison conditions
issues.description: The slope analysis compares the 14-day pre-attempt trajectory against other episodes 'for which there is no theoretical expectation of temporal change.' But the comparison episodes are arbitrary two-week windows whose 'day 0' anchoring is not equivalent to the attempt anchor, so any difference in slope may reflect the anchoring/definition asymmetry rather than a true risk signal. This design asymmetry confounds the interaction interpretation.
issues.quote: compared to changes during other two-week periods for episode types of lower suicide risk (for which there is no theoretical expectation of temporal change)
